questions.question_text: A small town with a demand of $900\text{kW}$ of electric power at $220\text{V}$ is situated $20\text{km}$ away from an electric power generating station. Each wire of the two-wire transmission line has a resistance per unit length of $5 \times 10^{-4}\Omega\text{m}^{-1}$ . The town gets power from the line through a $45000\text{V}$ to $220\text{V}$ step-down transformer at a substation in the town. The line power loss in the form of heat is:
questions.question_html: A small town with a demand of $900\text{kW}$ of electric power at $220\text{V}$ is situated $20\text{km}$ away from an electric power generating station. Each wire of the two-wire transmission line has a resistance per unit length of $5 \times 10^{-4}\Omega\text{m}^{-1}$ . The town gets power from the line through a $45000\text{V}$ to $220\text{V}$ step-down transformer at a substation in the town. The line power loss in the form of heat is:
questions.explanation_text: The town receives power through a step-down transformer whose primary voltage is $45000\text{V}$ . The power demand of the town is $P=900\text{kW}=900000\text{W}$ So the current in the transmission line is $I=\frac{P}{V}$ $I=\frac{900000}{45000}=20\text{A}$ Now, each wire is $20\text{km}$ long. $20\text{km}=20000\text{m}$ Resistance per unit length of each wire is $5 \times 10^{-4}\Omega\text{m}^{-1}$ So resistance of one wire is $R=5 \times 10^{-4} \times 20000$ $R=10\Omega$ Since it is a two-wire transmission line, total resistance is $R_{\text{total}}=10+10=20\Omega$ Power loss in the line as heat is $P_{\text{loss}}=I^{2}R$ $P_{\text{loss}}=(20)^{2} \times 20$ $P_{\text{loss}}=400 \times 20=8000\text{W}$ $P_{\text{loss}}=8\text{kW}$ So the line power loss is $8\text{kW}$ Correct option: Option B .
questions.explanation_html:
The town receives power through a step-down transformer whose primary voltage is $45000\text{V}$ .

The power demand of the town is

$P=900\text{kW}=900000\text{W}$

So the current in the transmission line is

$I=\frac{P}{V}$

$I=\frac{900000}{45000}=20\text{A}$

Now, each wire is $20\text{km}$ long.

$20\text{km}=20000\text{m}$

Resistance per unit length of each wire is

$5 \times 10^{-4}\Omega\text{m}^{-1}$

So resistance of one wire is

$R=5 \times 10^{-4} \times 20000$

$R=10\Omega$

Since it is a two-wire transmission line, total resistance is

$R_{\text{total}}=10+10=20\Omega$

Power loss in the line as heat is

$P_{\text{loss}}=I^{2}R$

$P_{\text{loss}}=(20)^{2} \times 20$

$P_{\text{loss}}=400 \times 20=8000\text{W}$

$P_{\text{loss}}=8\text{kW}$

So the line power loss is

$8\text{kW}$

Correct option: Option B.

questions.explanation_text: In a circuit containing a pure resistor connected to an AC source, the voltage and current remain in the same phase. For a pure resistor, Ohm’s law applies at every instant: $V=IR$ If the applied AC voltage is $V=V_{0}sin\omega t$ then the current is $I=\frac{V}{R}=\frac{V_{0}}{R}sin\omega t$ So, $I=I_{0}sin\omega t$ Both voltage and current vary as $sin\omega t$ . This means they reach zero, maximum, and minimum values at the same time. So, the phase difference between voltage and current is $0^{\circ}$ Hence, the correct option is: $\text{Option C: Voltage and current are in same phase with each other}$
questions.explanation_html:
In a circuit containing a pure resistor connected to an AC source, the voltage and current remain in the same phase.

For a pure resistor, Ohm’s law applies at every instant:

$V=IR$

If the applied AC voltage is

$V=V_{0}sin\omega t$

then the current is

$I=\frac{V}{R}=\frac{V_{0}}{R}sin\omega t$

So,

$I=I_{0}sin\omega t$

Both voltage and current vary as $sin\omega t$ . This means they reach zero, maximum, and minimum values at the same time.

So, the phase difference between voltage and current is

$0^{\circ}$

Hence, the correct option is:

$\text{Option C: Voltage and current are in same phase with each other}$

questions.question_html: A sinusoidal voltage produced by an AC generator at any instant t is given by an equation $V=311sin314$ t. The rms value of voltage and frequency are respectively
questions.explanation_text: The sinusoidal voltage from an AC generator at any instant is represented by the equation $V=311sin314t$ . To determine the root mean square (rms) value of the voltage, we use the formula for the rms value of a sinusoidal voltage: $V_{\text{rms}}=\frac{V_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{311}{\sqrt{2}}=220\text{V}$ Here, $V_{0}=311\text{V}$ is the peak voltage. To find the frequency, we use the relationship between angular frequency ( $\omega$ ) and frequency ( $f$ ): $\omega=2\pi f$ Given $\omega=314$ , we set: $314=2\pi f$ Solving for $f$ , we find: $f=\frac{314}{2\pi} \approx 50\text{Hz}$ Thus, the rms value of the voltage is 220 V, and the frequency is 50 Hz.
questions.explanation_html:
The sinusoidal voltage from an AC generator at any instant is represented by the equation $V=311sin314t$ .

To determine the root mean square (rms) value of the voltage, we use the formula for the rms value of a sinusoidal voltage:

$V_{\text{rms}}=\frac{V_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{311}{\sqrt{2}}=220\text{V}$

Here, $V_{0}=311\text{V}$ is the peak voltage.

To find the frequency, we use the relationship between angular frequency ( $\omega$ ) and frequency ( $f$ ):

$\omega=2\pi f$

Given $\omega=314$ , we set:

$314=2\pi f$

Solving for $f$ , we find:

$f=\frac{314}{2\pi} \approx 50\text{Hz}$

Thus, the rms value of the voltage is 220 V, and the frequency is 50 Hz.

questions.question_text: The frequency of an alternating current is $50Hz$ . What is the minimum time taken by current to reach its peak value from rms value?
questions.question_html: The frequency of an alternating current is $50Hz$ . What is the minimum time taken by current to reach its peak value from rms value?
questions.explanation_text: Given, Frequency of an alternating current, $f=50Hz$ If $t_{1}$ be the time at rms value of alternating current, then $\begin{aligned} & I_{rms}=I_{0}sin\omega t_{1}\text{or}\frac{I_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}=I_{0}sin\omega t_{1} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=sin\omega t_{1} \Rightarrow sin\frac{\pi}{4}=sin\omega t_{1} \Rightarrow t_{1}=\frac{\pi}{4\omega}\text{.... (i)} \end{aligned}$ Similarly, If $t_{2}$ be time at peak value of alternating current, then $I_{0}=I_{0}sin\omega t_{2}$ $\begin{aligned} 1 & =sin\omega t_{2} \\ sin\frac{\pi}{2} & =sin\omega t_{2} \Rightarrow \omega t_{2}=\frac{\pi}{2} \\ t_{2} & =\frac{\pi}{2\omega} \end{aligned}$ $\therefore$ Minimum time taken by current to reach its peak value from rms value $\begin{aligned} & =t_{2}-t_{1}=\frac{\pi}{2\omega}-\frac{\pi}{4\omega}=\frac{\pi}{4\omega} \\ & =\frac{\pi}{4 \times 2 \times \pi \times 50}=\frac{1}{400}=2.5 \times 10^{-3}s \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given, Frequency of an alternating current, $f=50Hz$

If $t_{1}$ be the time at rms value of alternating current, then

$\begin{aligned} & I_{rms}=I_{0}sin\omega t_{1}\text{or}\frac{I_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}=I_{0}sin\omega t_{1} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=sin\omega t_{1} \Rightarrow sin\frac{\pi}{4}=sin\omega t_{1} \Rightarrow t_{1}=\frac{\pi}{4\omega}\text{.... (i)} \end{aligned}$

Similarly, If $t_{2}$ be time at peak value of alternating current, then $I_{0}=I_{0}sin\omega t_{2}$

$\begin{aligned} 1 & =sin\omega t_{2} \\ sin\frac{\pi}{2} & =sin\omega t_{2} \Rightarrow \omega t_{2}=\frac{\pi}{2} \\ t_{2} & =\frac{\pi}{2\omega} \end{aligned}$

$\therefore$ Minimum time taken by current to reach its peak value from rms value

$\begin{aligned} & =t_{2}-t_{1}=\frac{\pi}{2\omega}-\frac{\pi}{4\omega}=\frac{\pi}{4\omega} \\ & =\frac{\pi}{4 \times 2 \times \pi \times 50}=\frac{1}{400}=2.5 \times 10^{-3}s \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: In domestic AC supplies like in Karnataka, the 220 V is not the peak voltage but the effective (or RMS: root mean square) value of the voltage. Meanwhile, 50 Hz indicates that the AC voltage completes 50 cycles every second. Let’s break it down: Effective (RMS) Voltage: For a sinusoidal voltage, the effective value is calculated from the peak value using the formula: $V_{\text{rms}}=\frac{V_{\text{peak}}}{\sqrt{2}}$ Thus, a 220 V RMS value corresponds to a peak voltage of approximately 311 V. The RMS value is used because it reflects the equivalent DC voltage in terms of the power delivered. Frequency: The 50 Hz means the AC voltage cycles 50 times per second. It is simply the standard frequency of the alternating current and is not an angular frequency (which would be measured in radians per second). Considering the options: Option A: Incorrect because 220 V is not the peak value. Option B: Indicates "ms value of voltage and frequency". Here, "ms" is intended to represent the effective (RMS) value. This is the correct interpretation. Option C: Incorrect because the mean (or average) value of a pure AC sinusoid over a complete cycle is zero. Option D: Incorrect because 220 V is not a peak value and 50 Hz is not an angular frequency. Therefore, the correct choice is Option B.
questions.explanation_html:
In domestic AC supplies like in Karnataka, the 220 V is not the peak voltage but the effective (or RMS: root mean square) value of the voltage. Meanwhile, 50 Hz indicates that the AC voltage completes 50 cycles every second. Let’s break it down:

Effective (RMS) Voltage:

For a sinusoidal voltage, the effective value is calculated from the peak value using the formula:

$V_{\text{rms}}=\frac{V_{\text{peak}}}{\sqrt{2}}$

Thus, a 220 V RMS value corresponds to a peak voltage of approximately 311 V.

The RMS value is used because it reflects the equivalent DC voltage in terms of the power delivered.

Frequency:

The 50 Hz means the AC voltage cycles 50 times per second.

It is simply the standard frequency of the alternating current and is not an angular frequency (which would be measured in radians per second).

Considering the options:

Option A: Incorrect because 220 V is not the peak value.

Option B: Indicates "ms value of voltage and frequency". Here, "ms" is intended to represent the effective (RMS) value. This is the correct interpretation.

Option C: Incorrect because the mean (or average) value of a pure AC sinusoid over a complete cycle is zero.

Option D: Incorrect because 220 V is not a peak value and 50 Hz is not an angular frequency.

Therefore, the correct choice is Option B.

options.label: A
B

questions.explanation_text: Explanation Inductive reactance, denoted as $X_{L}$ , is given by the formula: $X_{L}=\omega L=2\pi vL$ where: $\omega$ is the angular frequency, $L$ is the inductance, $v$ is the frequency of the voltage source. This equation shows that the inductive reactance is directly proportional to the frequency ( $v$ ) of the voltage source. Therefore, as the frequency increases, the inductive reactance $X_{L}$ also increases linearly. Thus, the relationship between $X_{L}$ and $v$ is linear, implying that when plotted on a graph, it should form a straight line with a positive slope.
questions.explanation_html:
Explanation

Inductive reactance, denoted as $X_{L}$ , is given by the formula:

$X_{L}=\omega L=2\pi vL$

where:

$\omega$ is the angular frequency,

$L$ is the inductance,

$v$ is the frequency of the voltage source.

This equation shows that the inductive reactance is directly proportional to the frequency ( $v$ ) of the voltage source. Therefore, as the frequency increases, the inductive reactance $X_{L}$ also increases linearly.

Thus, the relationship between $X_{L}$ and $v$ is linear, implying that when plotted on a graph, it should form a straight line with a positive slope.

questions.question_html: A 100 W bulb is connected to an AC source of $220V,50Hz$ . Then, the current flowing through the bulb is
questions.explanation_text: To find the current flowing through the bulb, we use the power formula for resistive loads: $P=IV,$ where $P$ is the power (in watts), $I$ is the current (in amperes), $V$ is the voltage (in volts). Given: $P=100\text{W},$ $V=220\text{V}.$ We rearrange the equation to solve for $I$ : $I=\frac{P}{V}.$ Substitute the given values: $I=\frac{100}{220}=\frac{10}{22}=\frac{5}{11}\text{A}.$ So, the current flowing through the bulb is $\frac{5}{11}\text{A}$ , which corresponds to Option A.

questions.question_html: In the series $L-C-R$ circuit, the power dissipation is through
questions.explanation_text: In an ideal series L–C–R circuit, only the resistor dissipates power as heat. The inductor (L) and capacitor (C) store energy in their magnetic and electric fields, respectively, but do not dissipate it. Here's a brief explanation: The resistor (R) converts electrical energy into heat, and the power dissipated by it is given by $P=I^{2}R$ where $I$ is the current through the resistor. The inductor (L) and capacitor (C) temporarily store energy (in their magnetic and electric fields) and then return it to the circuit. They do not cause any net loss of energy. Thus, the power loss in the circuit is solely due to the resistor. If the options are interpreted as follows: Option A: R (power dissipated here) Option B: L Option C: C Option D: Both L and C Then the correct answer is Option A.

questions.question_text: A coil of inductive reactance $1/\sqrt{3}\Omega$ and resistance $1\Omega$ is connected to a $200V,50Hz$ AC supply. The time lag between maximum voltage and current is
questions.question_html: A coil of inductive reactance $1/\sqrt{3}\Omega$ and resistance $1\Omega$ is connected to a $200V,50Hz$ AC supply. The time lag between maximum voltage and current is
questions.explanation_text: The coil has an inductive reactance $X_{L}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\Omega$ and resistance $R=1\Omega$ . We need to determine the time lag between the maximum voltage and current when connected to a $200V,50Hz$ AC supply. To find this, we start by calculating the phase angle $\phi$ using the tangent of the phase angle: $tan\phi=\frac{X_{L}}{R}=\frac{1/\sqrt{3}}{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ Then, the phase angle $\phi$ is: $\phi=tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=30^{\circ}$ Now, we convert the phase angle to radians to find the time lag: $\omega t=\frac{\pi}{6}$ Solving for $t$ : $t=\frac{\pi}{6\omega}=\frac{\pi}{6 \times 2\pi f}$ Simplifying further: $t=\frac{1}{12f}$ Given the frequency $f=50Hz$ : $t=\frac{1}{12 \times 50}=\frac{1}{600}s$ Therefore, the time lag between maximum voltage and current is $\frac{1}{600}s$ .
questions.explanation_html:
The coil has an inductive reactance $X_{L}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\Omega$ and resistance $R=1\Omega$ . We need to determine the time lag between the maximum voltage and current when connected to a $200V,50Hz$ AC supply.

To find this, we start by calculating the phase angle $\phi$ using the tangent of the phase angle:

$tan\phi=\frac{X_{L}}{R}=\frac{1/\sqrt{3}}{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

Then, the phase angle $\phi$ is:

$\phi=tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=30^{\circ}$

Now, we convert the phase angle to radians to find the time lag:

$\omega t=\frac{\pi}{6}$

Solving for $t$ :

$t=\frac{\pi}{6\omega}=\frac{\pi}{6 \times 2\pi f}$

Simplifying further:

$t=\frac{1}{12f}$

Given the frequency $f=50Hz$ :

$t=\frac{1}{12 \times 50}=\frac{1}{600}s$

Therefore, the time lag between maximum voltage and current is $\frac{1}{600}s$ .

questions.question_html: The output of a step down transformers is measured to be 48 V when connected to a 12 W bulb. The value of peak current is
questions.explanation_text: Given: Output of the step-down transformer, $V_{s}=48\text{V}$ Power associated with the secondary coil, $P_{s}=12\text{W}$ To find the current in the secondary coil, use the formula: $I_{s}=\frac{P_{s}}{V_{s}}=\frac{12}{48}=\frac{1}{4}=0.25\text{A}$ The amplitude of the current, $I_{0}$ , is calculated as follows: $I_{0}=I_{s}\sqrt{2}=0.25 \times \sqrt{2}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\text{A}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given:

Output of the step-down transformer, $V_{s}=48\text{V}$

Power associated with the secondary coil, $P_{s}=12\text{W}$

To find the current in the secondary coil, use the formula:

$I_{s}=\frac{P_{s}}{V_{s}}=\frac{12}{48}=\frac{1}{4}=0.25\text{A}$

The amplitude of the current, $I_{0}$ , is calculated as follows:

$I_{0}=I_{s}\sqrt{2}=0.25 \times \sqrt{2}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\text{A}$
